prompt: Which component of a series repeats with a period you could name before looking at the data?

choices.text: The cycle, because it also rises and falls again and again
choices.why: A cycle repeats without a fixed length, so nobody can name its period in advance.

choices.text: Seasonality
choices.why: Right. Seven days, twelve months, twenty-four hours: the period is tied to the calendar.

choices.text: The trend
choices.why: The trend is the long direction and does not repeat at all.

choices.text: The noise, once it has been averaged
choices.why: Averaging removes noise; it does not turn it into a pattern.

prompt: Panela took 351,453 orders in 2023, 450,836 in 2024 and 505,927 in 2025. What do the totals say about the trend?

choices.text: Growth that is slowing
choices.why: Right. The second rise, 55,091, is smaller than the first, 99,383.

choices.text: Growth that is speeding up, because each year is higher than the last
choices.why: Each year is higher, but by less each time. Higher is not faster.

choices.text: No trend: the rise is the yearly season
choices.why: A yearly total holds every season once, so the season cannot move it.

choices.text: Nothing yet, since three totals are too few to say anything at all
choices.why: Three totals are too few to separate a trend from a long cycle, but they do show the direction and that it is slowing.

prompt: A manager asks whether last Monday, with 1,350 orders, was a good day. Which component does the question really ask about?

choices.text: The trend, since good means above the long direction
choices.why: Above the trend is not enough: a Monday is always above an average day, because of the weekly season.

choices.text: The weekly season
choices.why: The season says what a Monday usually is. The question is how this Monday differed from that.

choices.text: The cycle
choices.why: A cycle lasts years; one day says nothing about it.

choices.text: The noise, once trend and season are removed
choices.why: Right. What made this Monday good or bad is what is left after the usual level and the usual Monday are taken away.

prompt: Across the three years a Monday averages 1,401 orders and a Saturday 1,028. How many more orders does an average Monday have?
Which question tells a season from a cycle before any model is run?

choices.text: Are the rises bigger than the falls?
choices.why: That describes a trend under the movement, and says nothing about whether the movement keeps time.

choices.text: Does the pattern appear in more than one year?
choices.why: A cycle can appear in several years too. What matters is whether it keeps a fixed length.

choices.text: Could the peaks have been marked on a calendar a year ago?
choices.why: Right. A season is tied to the calendar; a cycle's next turn is not.

choices.text: Is the swing larger than the noise?
choices.why: Both seasons and cycles can be larger than the noise.

prompt: A series rose for all three years of its data. A director asks whether that is a trend or the upswing of a cycle. What is the honest answer?

choices.text: A trend, because it never fell
choices.why: The upswing of a cycle longer than the data never falls inside the data either.

choices.text: Three years cannot tell them apart
choices.why: Right. A cycle longer than the data looks exactly like a trend.

choices.text: A cycle, because growth always ends
choices.why: That is a belief about the world, not something these three years show.

choices.text: Whichever one a decomposition of the three years reports, since that is what it is for
choices.why: A decomposition of three years merges them into one component; it cannot report what it cannot see.

prompt: Why does Panela's weekly pattern vanish from a table of monthly totals?

choices.text: Each month holds about four of every weekday
choices.why: Right. Aggregating over a whole number of periods removes a season.

choices.text: pandas smooths a monthly total with a moving average before printing it
choices.why: A sum is not a smoother. The pattern cancels because of what the month contains.

choices.text: The weekly pattern is noise
choices.why: It repeats every seven days for three years, which noise never does.

choices.text: Months differ in length
choices.why: That leaves a small weekday imbalance; it is not why the pattern vanishes.

prompt: Which of these are calendar effects that a fixed period of twelve months does NOT capture? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Carnival, which fell in February in 2024 and in March in 2025
choices.why: Right. It moves between months.

choices.text: Christmas landing on a different weekday each year
choices.why: Right. The date is fixed, the weekday is not, and Panela's week matters.

choices.text: January being quieter than December
choices.why: That happens in the same month every year, which is exactly what a twelve-month season holds.

choices.text: Monday being busier than Saturday
choices.why: That is the weekly season, a fixed period of seven days.

prompt: After removing trend and seasons, the leftovers still rise every Monday and dip every Saturday. What does that say?

choices.text: The leftovers are working: noise can look like anything
choices.why: Noise with a weekly rhythm is not noise. Something with a seven-day period is still in it.

choices.text: There is a cycle of one week
choices.why: A seven-day period is fixed and on the calendar, so it is a season by definition.

choices.text: The trend was too stiff
choices.why: A stiff trend leaves a slow wave behind, not a weekly one.

choices.text: The weekly season is still in them
choices.why: Right. A pattern in the leftovers means a component was missed.

prompt: Why does the course install its packages into a virtual environment rather than into the system's Python?

choices.text: A virtual environment runs programs faster
choices.why: Speed is the same; the interpreter is the same program.

choices.text: pip refuses to install anything at all unless a virtual environment is active
choices.why: pip works elsewhere; recent Linux refuses it for the system's Python, which is a different thing.

choices.text: It leaves the system's packages alone and holds the pinned versions
choices.why: Right. Recent distributions refuse installs into the system's Python for the first reason.

choices.text: statsmodels requires it
choices.why: No package requires a virtual environment.

choices.text: .venv\bin\python

choices.text: .venv\Scripts\python

choices.text: python3, since Windows has no virtual environments
choices.why: Windows has them; they are laid out differently.

choices.text: py -m venv
choices.why: That creates an environment; it does not run a program in one.

prompt: Why do the yearly totals in look.py show the trend and not the seasons?

choices.text: groupby removes seasonality
choices.why: groupby only groups. What cancels the seasons is what each group contains.

choices.text: The seasons are too small to see in a total
choices.why: January is about a quarter quieter than July; that is not small. It cancels, which is different.

choices.text: A year holds each season whole, so they cancel
choices.why: Right. A whole period of a season adds up to the same thing every year.

choices.text: A sum always hides every pattern in a series, whatever period it is taken over
choices.why: A sum over a month hides the week and keeps the year. It depends on the period summed over.

prompt: In look.py's monthly means for 2024, June to December are almost flat and well above January to March. Why can one year not say whether July is a busy month?

choices.text: Because July has school holidays in Brazil
choices.why: That might be a reason for a season; it does not explain why one year cannot measure it.

choices.text: The business grew during the year, so a later month is higher whatever its season
choices.why: Right. The trend leaks into the season, and lesson 2 separates them.

choices.text: Means are the wrong statistic; medians would separate them
choices.why: A median of a growing year is just as contaminated by the growth.

choices.text: Twelve months are too few to compute a mean
choices.why: Each mean averages about thirty days. The problem is what the months are compared against.

choices.text: Is Panela bigger this year than last?
choices.why: Right. Whole years compared remove the seasons.

choices.text: Why is Monday busier than Saturday?
choices.why: That is the weekly season.

choices.text: Is growth slowing down?
choices.why: Right. It asks about the shape of the long direction.

choices.text: Was yesterday unusually quiet?
choices.why: That is about the noise, once trend and season are removed.

prompt: A rise and fall that repeats with no fixed period, like an economy expanding and contracting, is called a ___.
A forecast treats a three-year business cycle as if it were a season of three years. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, if the cycle really lasted three years last time
choices.why: The last cycle's length says nothing about the next one's; that is what makes it a cycle.

choices.text: It overestimates the noise
choices.why: The error is in timing a turn, not in the size of the noise.

choices.text: It predicts the next turn on schedule, and the turn comes at another time
choices.why: Right. A season can be projected from the calendar and a cycle cannot.

choices.text: It cannot be fitted, since seasons must be shorter than a year
choices.why: A season may be any fixed calendar length; the problem is that a cycle is not fixed.
